articles.title: College sports' eligibility crisis is sprawling well beyond LSU, football and basketball — 'It's beyond unfair. It's heartless.'
articles.summary: While some players who previously signed contracts in the NFL or NBA have been able to win state court rulings to return to college, others have been left in...
articles.body:
On Friday, the day he was scheduled to fly to Knoxville, Tennessee, to begin camp as a late addition to the Volunteers, Monty Hunt awoke in his San Diego home to a text.

A Tennessee staff member informed him that he was, as of that morning, no longer eligible.

How could he be eligible one day and not eligible another?

Upon opening social media, he got his answer: A federal appeals court ruled in favor of the NCAA by freezing a Colorado court's sweeping decision to grant all of the 2022 high school class members an additional fifth year of eligibility.

The appeals decision — to stay the lower court's order until the completion of a full appeals process — means that Hunt's lifelong dream, at least for now, is dashed. And so too is the $50,000 in promised NIL compensation and scholarship costs.

"It's stressful for sure," he told Yahoo Sports on Monday during an interview. "I was waiting all these months and I finally got a chance to play SEC ball and the day before I leave, it gets pulled."

The appeals court ruling dealt a stunning blow to hundreds of athletes across the college sports landscape who were preparing to play this fall season in their respective sport through the federal ruling out of Colorado.

They were actively practicing, some even had already participated in exhibition games. They were on depth charts, travel rosters, scholarship lists and even NIL payment plans. They are team captains, key backups and role players.

Out from under them all, the proverbial rug was pulled.

"I literally spent all day Friday crying," said Ocean Rideout, a Portland State soccer player.

In the middle of a multi-game exhibition trip to California last week, Rideout learned of the court's ruling from an assistant coach at breakfast, just a few hours after she started in a preseason match and hours before she was scheduled to start in another one.

"I was suspended from all team activities," she said. "It's emotionally distressing to be in a limbo situation. One day you are eligible and one day you are ineligible."

Like many athletes across the country, Rideout spent much of her weekend researching ways to file a lawsuit in state court to regain her eligibility. It beats waiting weeks or months for the completion of an appeals process in the federal case in Colorado.

College administrators and athletes say that's the biggest rub with all of this: Inconsistent judicial decisions create an uneven playing field.

Those athletes who did not file or win lawsuits in state court are at the mercy of the Colorado federal case. A mad scramble is now unfolding for athletes to file locally.

Most of these players are similarly situated as part of the 2022 high school class requesting a fifth season of eligibility — a move sparked by the NCAA's new eligibility policy to grant athletes the ability to play five seasons, not four as was the case under the previous policy. However, the NCAA — a membership association where schools create the rules — did not grant an exception to those four-year players graduating this spring.

With the sweeping federal, class-action ruling frozen, hundreds of athletes are now exploring state-wide lawsuits — at least those who can afford it.

"I'm trying to find an attorney that will do it pro bono," Rideout said. "I don't have NIL funds like some of the football players."

Some may be unable to do so, like Abby Jeffries, a track and field athlete at Long Island University. As a named plaintiff in the federal case, she is unlikely to win an individual state court lawsuit, her attorneys say.

"It's beyond unfair. It's heartless," Jeffries said of the NCAA's approach.

"What happened with the stay has been devastating to athletes all over the country," said Diana Florence, with Shumaker, Loop & Kendrick law firm and one of the leaders of a team of attorneys representing athletes in the Colorado federal case. "If these athletes were born one year later, they'd be greeted with open arms for next year's eligibility. The NCAA's mission is supposed to center on the best interest of the student athlete. In what way is preventing athletes like Abby Jeffries from competing consistent with that mission?"

The Colorado ruling sent Jeffries, an aspiring medical student, quite literally to the bank. She needed to extract a $30,000 loan now to cover tuition after her scholarship was revoked.

"It's a mess," said Darren Heitner, a Florida-based sports law attorney who claims he's received nearly 1,000 inquiries since Friday's ruling. He expects dozens of lawsuits to be filed this week from athletes seeking a fifth season of eligibility.

More than 18 eligibility lawsuits have already been filed in 15 different states by more than 150 athletes in response to the association not making an exception for those 2022 high school class members. The NCAA has won a stay in three: the federal court decision, one in Ohio and another in New Jersey.

No single suit has drawn more attention than a Louisiana judge's decision to grant a group of athletes a fifth year, including several of them who signed NFL undrafted free agent contracts and even competed in NFL preseason games.

At least two of those players hold agreements to join coach Lane Kiffin and the LSU football team: tight end Dae'Quan Wright from the Cleveland Browns and defensive lineman Zxavian Harris from the New Orleans Saints . Kiffin coached both last year at Ole Miss.

Though he was careful not to confirm any new signings, Kiffin addressed the situation during a regularly scheduled news conference on Monday, defending his program and other schools for recruiting players in the NFL. He pointed the finger at the current system .

Athletes are only using legal avenues to regain eligibility that they did not know would exist, he said. The NCAA did not vote to implement the new five-year eligibility policy until June. Many players were required to make the decision to turn professional months before that.

"Because of the [court] rulings, they are going to play for you or someone else," Kiffin said. "We made the decision to recruit them. It's wrong to be critical of these kids. They were granted a fifth year and a judge said they were wronged."

But his own conference is taking exception to his transactional moves.

Many players choose to file legally knowing they have an open roster spot at a specific school or schools. This often means that schools are supporting player lawsuits that are challenging the very rules that the schools themselves created.

In a hurriedly called virtual SEC presidents meeting on Monday night, the league's leaders unanimously supported opposition to professional players returning to college, even releasing a statement decrying such.

"College sports are for college athletes," one of the lines of the statement read.

Beyond the statement, university presidents and league officials are expected to direct their athletic departments against accepting players who signed professional contracts and competed in pro contests, or risk potential sanctions, according to those with knowledge of the meeting.

According to SEC bylaws, commissioner Greg Sankey and/or the conference's presidents hold authority to deem a player ineligible, fine or suspend school coaches and administrators, and even prohibit a program from competing in league games or the conference championship.

More discussion on these topics are expected during a joint, two-day meeting of SEC presidents and athletic directors in Birmingham that begins Tuesday — an unusual and significant gathering that was scheduled weeks ago, where officials plan to continue exploring a long-discussed conference-only governance model .

The eligibility fiasco is now expected to take center stage at a meeting that could turn tense and even heated.

LSU's new president, Wade Rousse, and athletic director, Verge Ausberry, are scheduled to attend. The program not only is in line to accept multiple professional football players. Men's basketball head coach Will Wade landed a big win Monday night: A Louisiana judge granted additional eligibility for RJ Luis to return to college . Luis, a member of the 2022 high school class, went undrafted during the 2025 NBA Draft, signed a two-way contract with the Utah Jazz, was traded to the Boston Celtics and played in three NBA games.

Awaiting Luis following the victory was none other than Wade, who embraced the player outside of the court room in an emotional moment caught by a local TV sports anchor from WBRZ. Wade landed a key piece for the inaugural team of his second stint in Baton Rouge.

Outside the courthouse in Baton Rouge on Monday, Luis' attorney, Elliot Abrams, described the NCAA's decision to permit schools to pay players directly as creating a "professional league," where "arbitrary" eligibility rules "don't stand up to reason."

"This is a judge forcing the NCAA to live up to the law," he told reporters.

During an interview on Monday, one college sports stakeholder described the situation as Sankey's "Sorsby moment," a reference to Brendan Sorsby and Texas Tech's legal entanglement with the Big 12. The conference filed suit against the school for its intentions to play a player who gambled on his own team.

If the SEC penalizes LSU or the professional athletes who plan to play there, will the school or those athletes file suit against the conference? Will the league file suit against its own school?

LSU may be aggressively signing these players at a higher clip than most, but the school isn't alone. In fact, just last week, a former Kentucky basketball player, Mark Mitchell, won a lawsuit for additional eligibility and is transferring to Missouri . This flies directly in the face of another SEC policy against intraconference transfers outside of the portal period.

On Monday, attorneys filed a motion to expedite the federal case in Colorado.

The goal: reach some sort of conclusion before the start of, or at least during, the fall sports season. It may be difficult. Football season kicks off this weekend.

The expedited motion is in an attempt to schedule oral arguments on the court's September calendar. If the judge declines or the calendar is full, that puts the case on the November calendar.

"We are doing everything we can to accelerate the briefing," said Rob Shelquist, another attorney on the case from Cuneo Gilbert Flannery & LaDuca. "If this drags to November, it is probably the end of the road for the fall athletes. If the court doesn't accelerate briefing and this languishes until November, we will still do everything we can to save the winter and spring athletes. The NCAA claims its mission is to create opportunities for athletes and yet we are the ones fighting to allow schools and coaches who want to fill open roster spots and award unused scholarships to these athletes."

Meanwhile, the inequalities will continue across the landscape.

For instance, Texas State has a football player on its roster, linebacker Treylin Payne, who's now ineligible after the Colorado decision. The Bobcats' season-opening opponent, Texas, will play in the game lineman Cole Hutson , who participated in minicamps with the Browns and Cowboys before winning a local eligibility lawsuit.

The players are in a similar situation as 2022 high school athletes seeking a fifth season of eligibility. Payne is expected, like so many others, to seek a state court ruling.

Coaches have publicly expressed varying degrees of opinions on the situation.

Some, like Oregon 's Dan Lanning, rebuff the notion of recruiting pro players.

"Once you go to the NFL, to me, you're in the NFL. You don't get the opportunity to come back," Lanning said.

But others, like Ohio State's Ryan Day, suggested that he'd consider NFL players who formerly played who are granted eligibility. "Do I like anything about it? Absolutely not, but we gotta do what's right for Ohio State," Day said.

Meanwhile, NCAA executives and the power conference commissioners continue to hold conversations on their approach and options. There is no easy solution for the situation, administrators say, but there are several options to consider.

Leaders could issue a broad waiver to grant all members of the 2022 high school class eligibility, but that likely means creating a transfer portal for movement and exceptions for roster caps. Those are moves that school executives declined to make in May — a reason that an exception wasn't made to begin with.

This move also does not solve another festering problem for college officials: the ban on professional players returning to college, which is now under attack within these eligibility lawsuits.

Leaders could decide to continue to litigate individual state and federal court cases, hoping for more friendly judicial decisions or appeals court victories like the one in Colorado. But this is costly, time-consuming and creates the current uneven playing field.

Another option has emerged, too: conferences taking matters into their own hands by creating league policies and enforcing them from the conference office. This dovetails with this week's meetings in Birmingham as leaders consider and view presentations of league-wide governance in an effort to limit the amount of legal challenges.

In fact, all four power leagues are expected to consider such a rule — something that may put the conferences at the center of new lawsuits, rather than the NCAA.

In the meantime, it isn't just football and basketball players chasing hundreds of thousands of dollars who are caught in the quagmire. Soccer, field hockey and track athletes are mired in what one person calls the "NCAA Trap."

"It's beyond unfair," said Jeffries, the track athlete at Long Island who now needs a bank loan to enroll in classes. "My coaches told me, 'We have the [scholarship] money for you! We just can't do it!'"

articles.title: Nuggets Unveil New Floor Design in Video, Photo Ahead of 2026-27 NBA Season
articles.summary: The Denver Nuggets revealed the team's new floor design for the 2026-27 season on Tuesday.
articles.body:
The Denver Nuggets revealed the team's new floor design for the 2026-27 season on Tuesday.

The Nuggets showed off the court in a pair of posts on X.

Updates include a new two-toned hardwood design as well as the addition of a silhouette of the mountains behind Denver's skyline.

The Nuggets will enter their 2026-27 campaign looking to clinch a ninth consecutive playoff appearance after wrapping up a 54-28 finish last season.

articles.title: Arranca la era de Xavi Pascual en el Dubái Basketball
articles.standfirst: El técnico catalán dirige el primer entrenamiento con el equipo emiratí, cuyo ambicioso proyecto le sitúa entre los aspirantes a la Final Four de la Euroliga
articles.summary: El técnico catalán dirige el primer entrenamiento con el equipo emiratí, cuyo ambicioso proyecto le sitúa entre los aspirantes a la Final Four de la Euroliga
articles.body: La era Xavi Pascual ya ha comenzado en el Dubái Basketball. Tres semanas antes de que arranquen los partidos oficiales, el técnico ha dirigido el primer entrenamiento del ambicioso proyecto del conjunto emiratí, que en su segunda temporada en la Euroliga ya va con todo. Como muestra de ello, la incorporación del entrenador catalán, que pagó su cláusula de rescisión para salir del Barcelona y disfrutará de un gran contrato. Pascual ha encontrado en Dubái una plantilla y un músculo financiero que no tuvo durante su breve segunda etapa en Barcelona. A su regreso al Palau, se le prometieron recursos en forma de fichajes que nunca se concretaron ni siquiera cuando la plantilla se vio gravemente perjudicada por las lesiones. A sus 53 años, el interés desde Emiratos Árabes y el objetivo de luchar por la Euroliga le hizo dar el paso de iniciar su tercera etapa en el extranjero tras las vividas en el Panathinaikos y el Zenit de San Petersburgo. La lucha por el cetro europeo no es una quimera para un club que ha sido uno de los grandes agitadores del mercado. Junto a Pascual han llegado el ala-pívot Toko Shengelia, también procedente del Barcelona, el pívot Mamadi Diakite (Kosner Baskonia), el base Davion Mintz (Wurzburg), el escolta Elie Okobo y el alero Jaron Blossomgame, estos dos últimos pescados en la desbandada sufrida por el AS Mónaco. Un quinteto que se suma a todo lo bueno que ya había en la plantilla: Dzanan Musa, McKinley Wright, Dwayne Bacon, Justin Anderson, Davis Bertans, Mfiondu Kabengele, Filip Petrusev... Con Mam Jaiteh, que la temporada pasada se rompió el tendón de Aquiles, 18 jugadores a disposición de Pascual. articles.title: Kate Koval of Ukraine Leaves LSU Following the Tigers' Signing of a Russian Player
articles.summary: BATON ROUGE, La. (AP) — Ukrainian center Kate Koval is leaving LSU less than two weeks after the Tigers brought in a player from Russia.
articles.body:
BATON ROUGE, La. (AP) — Ukrainian center Kate Koval is leaving LSU less than two weeks after the Tigers brought in a player from Russia.

LSU coach Kim Mulkey said Monday night that the 6-foot-5 Koval was leaving for "personal reasons," adding that the program will "respect her privacy on her decision."

"We had a long talk about it, and it was a hard decision for her," Mulkey continued. "I know it is hard because she loves LSU. Kate is a great person. She has to do what she feels is right for her, and we fully support her in that. We all wish her the best."

Koval, who was born in Kyiv, began her college career at Notre Dame. She transferred before last season to LSU, where she averaged 8.3 points and 6.3 rebounds per game.

LSU recently signed Anna Minaeva, a 6-5 post player who previously played professionally with MBA Moscow.

Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and the two countries have been at war since.

articles.title: Klay Thompson, 36, on joining the Heat: 'a redemption season'
articles.summary: The 36-year-old guard agreed to a buyout with the Mavericks in order to sign with the Heat.
articles.body:
Veteran guard Klay Thompson had his introductory press conference on Tuesday, where he was officially presented with a No. 11 Miami Heat jersey.

Thompson briefly spoke to the media about why he pushed to sign with the Heat, noting he liked the franchise's competitive, demanding atmosphere . He added that he liked "the opportunity to play high-level basketball throughout the season and the chance to make a deep postseason run. I've tasted winning before, and there's nothing like it."

On a more personal note, the veteran guard previewed the 2026-27 season, saying that it was " a redemption season ," especially because even at 36 years old, he believes he can still compete at "a high level."

Thompson spent last season with the Dallas Mavericks . He played in 69 games, but largely in a support role, starting only eight games. He averaged 11.7 points per game, his lowest mark over the course of a season in his career.

The veteran's numbers have declined over the last three seasons. After averaging 21.9 points with the Golden State Warriors over 69 games in the 2022-23 season, he averaged 17.9, 14.0 and 11.7 points per game in the three seasons after.

Klay to Miami, DeMar to Denver! Atlanta Dream are ROLLING, Valkyries-Lynx takeaways + DeWanna Bonner landing spots

Brandon Williams, Warriors reportedly agree to 1-year, $2.6M contract

RJ Luis granted ruling to join LSU, return to college basketball after going undrafted in latest eligibility case

Thompson's role with Miami has yet to be determined, but it could be a mix of starting games and providing a veteran boost off the bench. Miami's other shooting guard in the mix for starts is Tim Hardaway Jr , who averaged 13.5 points over 80 games with the Denver Nuggets last season.

Hardaway is on a one-year, $6.065 million deal, while Thompson signed a two-year, $11.48 million deal that includes a player option for next season.

Thompson wasn't the biggest acquisition for the Heat this offseason. Miami acquired two-time MVP Giannis Antetokounmpo from the Milwaukee Bucks along with Bobby Portis in a trade for Tyler Herro , Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jacquez Jr., Kasparas Jakučionis, the draft rights to Nate Ament , three first-round draft picks (2026, '31 and '33), one pick swap (2030) and a 2033 second-round selection.

One possible Miami starting lineup would feature Davion Mitchell , Thompson, Andrew Wiggins (who signed a three-year, $64 million extension with the Heat), Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo .

articles.title: Enes Kanter Freedom, deemed to have ‘the potential to be a threat,’ barred from Sky arena after altercation
articles.summary: Chicago Sky team owner Michael Alter said Tuesday Enes Kanter Freedom is barred from Wintrust Arena after his altercation with Natasha Cloud on Sunday.
articles.body: Chicago Sky team owner Michael Alter said Tuesday Enes Kanter Freedom is barred from Wintrust Arena after his altercation with Natasha Cloud on Sunday. Alter made the comments in an address to beat writers. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! "He has demonstrated to us, unequivocally, that he has the potential to be a threat," Alter said, via ESPN. It’s unclear how Freedom was determined to be a "threat" and whether there are actions he could take to possibly clear himself as such. OutKick reached out to the Sky for further comment. The incident occurred in the third quarter of the Sky’s loss to the Indiana Fever. Cloud scored a bucket that led to the Fever calling a timeout. She directed her emotion toward Freedom, who was sitting near the basket at the Wintrust Arena. Freedom stood up and walked toward Cloud. Sky players and security had to get in between the two. Freedom was then escorted out of the arena and was unable to return for the rest of the game. He explained the situation to OutKick after the game. "Sophie Cunningham shot a three, and I put my hands up to celebrate," Freedom said. "Literally, a couple possessions later, Natasha came back and started screaming and yelling and said, ‘She’s not gonna sleep with you.’ "And I was like, ‘I am not trying to sleep with her. I’m just here to protect women and support her.’ And then, obviously, after that she started yapping, and she started to walk towards me, and literally I just got up, and then I was like, ‘I’m just here to protect women, and that’s all.’" Freedom was wearing a shirt that explained the definition of a woman. He said he believed the shirt contributed to Cloud’s outburst. "I was cheering for my friend Sophie because when she shot that three, I put my hands in the air," Freedom said. "A couple possessions later, she came back and said, ‘She’s not gonna sleep with you.’ And I was shocked. I was like, ‘Listen, I’m not trying to sleep with her. I think she’s awesome. She’s a good friend.’ But I think it has a lot to do with my shirt. "I was obviously wearing a shirt explaining what a woman is, and I think that had a lot to do with what she thinks about women. I think it triggered her a lot." Alter said Tuesday that Freedom began "chirping" at Cloud in the third quarter. "He began to chirp with her in the third quarter," Alter said, via Chicago State of Mind Sports. I would characterize it as trash talking, nothing personal. Basketball-related, but enough to get her attention, engage her, and in my opinion, to try to provoke her. OutKick reached out to Freedom's reps for a response to the Sky's decision. Cloud didn’t speak at the Sky’s postgame media availability. She fired off a message on Threads in support of the transgender community. "To every trans kid/person, You are apart of MY community & tribe. You belong. You’re loved. You’re seen. You’re perfect as you are. & you will always be protected by me," Cloud wrote. Cloud’s message appeared to be a swipe at Freedom, who announced his intentions to compete in the WNBA as players and coaches have spoken out about trans athletes in women and girls’ sports. As he entered the arena Sunday afternoon, he was berated by a mob of angry WNBA fans. articles.title: Charles Barkley says WNBA players 'just don't like' Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham
articles.summary: Charles Barkley says WNBA players dislike Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham, blaming a mix of jealousy, race, and sexuality for the hostility.
articles.body: Charles Barkley didn’t mince words while talking about Indiana Fever stars Caitlin Clark, Sophie Cunningham and the WNBA. "Those girls do not like Caitlin Clark or Sophie Cunningham," Barkley said, referring to the other players in the WNBA and their feelings toward two of the league’s most popular players. But Barkley didn’t think it was all about race. "Without regard for race, they just don’t like them," Barkley added. Barkley made those comments on "The Michael Smerconish Program" while the two discussed what Barkley called the WNBA’s "awful year." One of the incidents the pair talked about was DiJonai Carrington’s Flagrant 2 foul on Cunningham during the Aug. 8 game between the Fever and Chicago Sky. WNBA SUDDENLY WANTS TO STICK TO BASKETBALL AFTER YEARS OF MAKING POLITICS PART OF THE PRODUCT Carrington delivered a vicious blow to Cunningham's head as the Fever guard attempted a fast-break layup. Cunningham was left with a bloody mouth following the contact. Referees reviewed the play, upgraded the call from a Flagrant 1 to a Flagrant 2 and ejected Carrington. Shortly after her ejection, Carrington posted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" on social media and tagged the Fever. She later said she never claimed the Flagrant 2 itself was the result of white privilege, though she didn't explain what prompted the post. Cunningham called the foul "unnecessary," said she had "no beef" with Carrington, then called it intentional and accused Carrington of seeking attention. Barkley says Carrington’s post turned the foul into a racial debate Smerconish said he went looking for data on whether hard fouls between Black and White WNBA players occur more often than they should. He said he found a peer-reviewed study suggesting they happen at the rate one would expect, which led him to argue that the media is what turns those incidents into racial controversies. Barkley didn’t buy it. "No, no, you’re wrong, though," Barkley said. "The reason they made it black and white [was] when that girl tweeted ‘white privilege.’ That was stupid on her part." SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPEAKS OUT AGAINST DIJONAI CARRINGTON AFTER FLAGRANT FOUL AND 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' POST Barkley called it "a dirty play. Period." He said Carrington’s post turned it into a racial argument. "When you turn stuff to the internet, all the race hustlers start coming out. We have a ton of race hustlers out there, White and Black. Let me repeat that. White and Black," Barkley said. Smerconish then brought up Larry Bird and Magic Johnson, whose rivalry came with obvious racial undertones but helped turn the NBA into a massive national product. Barkley agreed those undertones existed. He said the difference was that Bird and Johnson respected each other. "There was always respect," Barkley said, before repeating himself for emphasis. "There was always respect." Barkley says WNBA resentment toward Clark and Cunningham goes beyond race Barkley didn't accuse Carrington, or any other WNBA player, of racism. He did, however, offer his own theory for the hostility toward Clark and Cunningham. "I’m not gonna get on here and call somebody a racist because I don’t have any proof," Barkley said. "Whether it’s race, sexuality, or whatever, there’s something going on there." He said Clark and Cunningham are simply good players, but he believes the resentment toward them comes from a mix of factors. "She’s just a really good basketball player. Same thing with Sophie. She’s a good player," Barkley said. "I think it has something to do with sexuality, race, and jealousy. I think it’s all three of them. I don’t know how you break up the percentages." Barkley said the WNBA’s bad publicity bothers him because he believes the league has a lot going for it. The WNBA is expanding, players are making more money under a new CBA, and the league has young stars who should be driving the conversation. Instead, Barkley said, the WNBA keeps finding itself wrapped up in hard fouls, social-media posts and arguments that have little to do with basketball. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Smerconish suggested the WNBA could benefit from the attention, invoking the old belief that there is no such thing as bad publicity. Barkley didn’t agree. "I don’t think it works like that anymore, Michael," Barkley said. "When’s the last time you heard something positive about the WNBA? I can’t even remember."

articles.title: Ohio State coach Ryan Day addresses NFL players returning to college football: 'We're in a different world'
articles.summary: Ohio State's Ryan Day calls on conferences to establish a roster lock deadline as former NFL players become eligible to play college football.
articles.body: Not everything about modern college football is perfect, but we can say this for it: it's never boring. After an offseason dominated by debate over the importance of strength of schedule and how it's defined, the changing of the guard between the SEC and Big Ten, potential involvement from the federal government in collegiate athletics, and even more NIL (name, image and likeness) concerns, there's now a new controversy, just a few days before the season starts. Thanks to a series of cases making their way through the courts as a result of the NCAA adding a fifth year of eligibility, several players who ended their "amateur" careers and went to the NFL are now eligible to return to the college football ranks. NCAA ROCKED BY COLORADO JUDGE'S 2022 CLASS ELIGIBILITY RULING THAT COULD RESHAPE COLLEGE SPORTS THIS YEAR Immediately, opportunistic coaches seized on the opportunity to add more physically developed and experienced players to their rosters. Led by new LSU Tigers head coach Lane Kiffin. This has led to a flood of conference calls and meetings among major conferences as to the propriety of players who signed with NFL teams being allowed to play college football. One of the most prominent voices in the sport, Ohio State Buckeyes head coach Ryan Day, added his perspective, highlighting the push and pull of factors dominating discussion. LSU’S LANE KIFFIN FIRES BACK AT NFL RETURNEE BACKLASH: BLAME THE NCAA, NOT US FOR RECRUITING PRO ATHLETES "I told myself I would stop saying this is crazy," Day told the media earlier this week. "So I’m not gonna say that. But to think that we’re in a situation where we’re this late in the season and our rosters are not locked in is frustrating at the very least. But I’m not gonna sit here and keep saying that. So what does that mean for us? That’s the bottom line. Well, I think, in my opinion, the conferences have to decide if there’s a point where their rosters have to be locked in. Because once some of these guys become available, adding them to the roster is going to provide advantage for certain teams. So we’re certainly having conversations. articles.title: Kyle Lowry-Inspired Logo Teased by Raptors in New Video After Star's NBA Retirement
articles.summary: The Toronto Raptors hinted at a new potential logo in honor of Kyle Lowry in a social media post on Tuesday.
articles.body:
The Toronto Raptors hinted at a new potential logo in honor of Kyle Lowry in a social media post on Tuesday.

Lowry, who announced his retirement this offseason after signing a one-day contract with the Raptors, spent nine seasons with the Raptors, averaging 17.5 points and 7.1 assists per game in that time while helping to lead the team to an NBA championship.

The team already announced that his No. 7 jersey would be retired.

"Kyle is the Toronto Raptors—he created an identity for the Raptors that we strive to uphold every time we take the floor, play hard and play to win, for your teammates, for Toronto and for Canada," general manager and executive vice-president Bobby Webster said in a statement after Lowry retired. "Put your body on the line. Take a charge, dive for a loose ball—do all the little things that don't always show up in the box score, but add up to a storied, celebrated career. Kyle was the ultimate competitor whose No. 7 will always be remembered with the Raptors very first championship, and it's our honor to raise it to the rafters, where it belongs."

articles.title: US Olympic hero Nancy Hogshead launches petition calling for WNBA to restrict gender eligibility
articles.summary: Nancy Hogshead's Change.org petition has over 11,000 signatures demanding the WNBA clarify eligibility rules to explicitly include only biological females.
articles.body: Three-time Olympic swimming gold medalist Nancy Hogshead is calling on the WNBA to explicitly restrict player eligibility to biological females. Hogshead recently launched a Change.org petition asking the league to clarify the meaning of "woman" in its eligibility rules. The petition has collected more than 11,000 signatures since its Aug. 14 launch. "We’re calling for the WNBA to clarify that its eligibility rules are for women only," Hogshead told Fox News Digital. "If you wanna participate, you have to be a certain age, and you have to be a female." CHARLES BARKLEY DECLARES WNBA IS 'FOR WOMEN ONLY' AFTER ONGOING TRANSGENDER ATHLETE DEBATE Hogshead said she hopes the petition ultimately reaches 100,000 signatures. "It’s an 80/20 issue across the country, so we can do it," she said. "We have well over a million people who’ve engaged with our materials that we put out about the petition. We just gotta get them to sign on." The WNBA’s 2026 collective bargaining agreement states that "only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA." However, the agreement does not further define "woman" or include specific language addressing gender identity or sex assigned at birth. The debate intensified after former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White announced plans to enter the 2027 WNBA Draft while claiming to identify as women. League sources hav since said that neither of them is eligible and characterized their announcements as "publicity stunts." Hogshead said the declarations exposed what she considers a contradiction in policies based on gender self-identification. SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPEAKS OUT ON PROTECTING GIRLS FROM COMPETING AGAINST 'BIOLOGICAL MEN' "I love it that they came forward because it just shows the hypocrisy of the WNBA, and it shows the hypocrisy of gender ideology," Hogshead said. "For them to come forward and, you know, threaten to play in the WNBA and show up for the draft, it just shows just how ridiculous that gender ideology is." The WNBA previously said there were "no immediate eligibility matters" affecting the league and denounced "bad-faith efforts" to use the debate to "demean or marginalize others." Commissioner Cathy Engelbert also said league officials would continue discussing the subject with the players’ union and other stakeholders. Hogshead’s petition comes amid rallies outside WNBA games supporting Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham, who publicly opposed transgender participation in girls’ and women’s sports earlier this summer. "I really appreciate her for the stand that she has taken on behalf of women," Hogshead said of Cunningham. "If anything, the more people see of Sophie Cunningham, the more they like her." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Hogshead won three gold medals and one silver medal at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics. She later became a civil rights attorney and founded Champion Women, an organization that advocates for women and girls in athletics.

articles.title: Klay Thompson drops scary Heat & Giannis Antetokounmpo championship proclamation
articles.summary: Klay Thompson knows that the Heat led by Giannis Antetokounmpo are on the road for an NBA championship run and even he dropped a huge promise.
articles.body:
Klay Thompson drops scary Heat & Giannis Antetokounmpo championship proclamation originally appeared on The Sporting News . Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here .

Just when everyone thought that the Miami Heat were already scary with Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo , they got another daunting acquisition. Klay Thompson decided to join the party in South Beach so that he could get a fifth NBA championship under his belt. How confident is the former Dallas Mavericks and Golden State Warriors sharpshooter that he will be able to play at a championship-level once again? Simply put, he is very certain.

Thompson proclaims big championship-level jump to help Antetokounmpo, Heat

Klay Thompson has been far from his championship-caliber form for a while now. The last time that he was able to score more than 20 points on average in the regular season was during the 2022-23 NBA regular season, a year removed from the Warriors' most recent title run. Since then, he has settled for spot-up shooter roles and taught shooting mechanics to younger players on his squads. Thompson aims to change that with the Heat .

He plans to return to form heading into the 2026-27 NBA season and become the perfect complement to Giannis Antetokounmpo. The veteran sharpshooter declared all of this during his introductory press conference.

"I still think I can do it at a high level. Like you said, the durability has been, for me, a huge plus. You know, that's one thing that might have been questioned from all that time I had off. But, for me, all of those injuries are back in the past. I don't even think about them anymore. It's nice to be able to walk on the floor and play free-minded," Thompson declared.

In his most recent season with the Mavericks, Thompson looked like a shell of his former self. He hit a career-low average of 11.7 points while only knocking down 38.3% of his shots from three-point range. Despite that, he has shown strong durability by playing 69 regular-season games, which Antetokounmpo and the Heat could use in the coming season.

In the bigger picture, this move to acquire Thompson makes a lot of sense. With Tyler Herro and Jaime Jaquez Jr. now off the roster, the Heat need someone who can knock down shots. Schematically, Coach Erik Spoelstra has balanced out their inside and outside scoring. This is why the Heat ranked 10th in the league with their 36.4% field goal percentage. With Antetokounmpo joining the Heat, the need to have an elite spot-up shooter has become more apparent. This is because of the gravity the Greek Freak brings when driving inside the paint.

There is still so much to iron out in terms of rotations along with X's and O's. One thing is certain, however: the Heat need Thompson to equal his production from at least that 2022 Warriors NBA Championship run to hoist the Larry O'Brien trophy.

articles.title: Sky Owner Announced Enes Kanter Decision After Altercation
articles.summary: The Chicago Sky found themselves in the middle of a news cycle involving one of their players and former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom.During the second hal...
articles.body:
The Chicago Sky found themselves in the middle of a news cycle involving one of their players and former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom.

During the second half of the Sky's 113-90 loss to the Indiana Fever , Sky guard Natasha Cloud got into a verbal altercation with Kanter, who was sitting courtside with a shirt reading "WOMAN noun. adult human female." Security at Wintrust Arena then escorted Kanter from the game.

Kanter has since posted on social media and appeared on television defending himself. A new perspective is being told by the owner of the Sky.

Chicago Sky Owner Discusses Enes Kanter Freedom Controversy

GettyCHICAGO, ILLINOIS – AUGUST 23: Former basketball player Enes Kanter Freedom looks on during the second half between the Chicago Sky and the Indiana Fever at Wintrust Arena on August 23, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images)

Sky owner Michael Alter met with the local media on Tuesday to discuss the incident. According to Front Office Sports' Colin Salao, Kanter's manager texted Sky general manager Jeff Pagliocca that Kanter was coming to the game. Alter said that Pagliocca has not talked to Kanter in "three or four years."

Chicago Sky owner Michael Alter is meeting with local Chicago Sky beat writers and local Chicago media. — Colin Salao (@colincsalao) August 25, 2026

Chicago Sky owner Michael Alter is meeting with local Chicago Sky beat writers and local Chicago media.

— Colin Salao (@colincsalao) August 25, 2026

After that, Alter made it clear that Kanter's intentions were to be "provocative and just see how much attention he could get," but added he did not know where he was sitting before the game. Alter even spoke to people who were sitting near him to get the story.

"They each confirmed that the dialogue between Cloud and Kanter started with Kanter. He began to chirp with her sometime in the third quarter. I would characterize it as trash talking, nothing personal. Basketball-related, but enough to get her attention and to engage her, and in my opinion, to try to provoke her." "He portrays as this victimless person who did nothing, said nothing. Just wearing a t-shirt … We have five different security authorities that all agreed very quickly to throw him out because he made himself into a threat."

"They each confirmed that the dialogue between Cloud and Kanter started with Kanter. He began to chirp with her sometime in the third quarter. I would characterize it as trash talking, nothing personal. Basketball-related, but enough to get her attention and to engage her, and in my opinion, to try to provoke her."

"He portrays as this victimless person who did nothing, said nothing. Just wearing a t-shirt … We have five different security authorities that all agreed very quickly to throw him out because he made himself into a threat."

Alter announced that Kanter will no longer be allowed at Wintrust Arena "unless sometime in the future, he's able to prove to us that he's able to abide by our rules without being a potential threat." Alter's only regret is that he didn't tell the Sky players before the game, since it was close to tipoff.

Enes Kanter Won't Be Allowed at Chicago Sky Games Moving Forward

GettyAmerican basketball player Enes Kanter Freedom poses during an interview with AFP at the United Nations Office in Geneva on April 5, 2022. Enes Kanter Freedom, whose human rights advocacy has ruffled feathers, hopes to bend UN human rights chief Michelle Bachelet's ear on Thursday about her forthcoming China visit. (Photo by Fabrice COFFRINI / AFP via Getty Images)

This follows conversations about transgender women in sports, first raised by Fever guard Sophie Cunningham . Kanter and other former NBA players joined the conversation by saying they were "declaring" for the 2027 WNBA Draft. The league has since said he and the other players are not eligible.

No other WNBA teams have announced whether they will take action on it. As of the release of this article, Kanter did not respond to the news.

The Chicago Sky are back in action Tuesday to face the Connecticut Sun . They will then face the New York Liberty on Saturday before entering the World Cup break.
